faqs.q: Can exclusion work be done on a historic Annapolis home without damaging it?
faqs.a: Yes, and in the historic district it has to be. Slate roofs, soft old brick, and original trim around the State House and Academy neighborhoods do not tolerate careless fasteners or smeared sealant. We fit chimney caps, vent screens, and one-way exits to the existing openings, match mortar and flashing work to the building, and seal bat gaps with materials that can be removed cleanly later. The inspection comes first, because on a 150-year-old roofline the entry is often a settled joint or a rotted fascia board rather than a hole an animal chewed, and the repair list is different for each.

faqs.q: What is getting into crawlspaces in Eastport and West Annapolis?
faqs.a: Most often it is skunks and opossums living under waterfront homes and sheds, entering through broken or rusted crawlspace vents on the creek side of the house. Raccoons use the same openings when they are large enough, and in spring a female may den there with pups. We check who is actually home before anything is screened, remove the animals with low-stress handling, and replace the vent covers with anchored, corrosion-resistant screening suited to a brackish waterfront. Leaving one vent open on the Spa Creek side undoes the whole job, so every low opening gets checked, not just the one with tracks.

Annapolis.wildlife_intro:
Annapolis packs three centuries of housing around a working harbor, and the wildlife calls change block by block. In the historic district, brick colonials and Victorians near the State House and the Naval Academy have slate roofs, box gutters, and chimney tops that raccoons and bats have used for generations, while Eastport's maritime streets add boathouses and low waterfront sheds where skunks and opossums den underneath.

The Severn River and Spa Creek put marsh and mature tree canopy right against those older rooflines, so gray squirrels move from the big street oaks onto roofs without touching the ground, and big brown bats work the gaps in aging soffits all summer. West Annapolis and Murray Hill bring early-1900s porches and detached garages that groundhogs undermine, and the newer subdivisions out toward Parole trade the harbor animals for deer-edge raccoons and attic squirrels. Waterfront crawlspaces stay damp and open to the outside through old vents, which is why so many Annapolis jobs start below the house rather than above it. The work here has to respect historic fabric: exclusion is fitted and sealed so the fix protects the home without scarring brickwork, trim, or slate that cannot be replaced like-for-like.

faqs.q: Why do animals keep getting into homes in Glen Burnie?
faqs.a: Glen Burnie sits in central Maryland on the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay, between Baltimore and Annapolis, and the habitat in between the houses — Magothy and South rivers — gives wildlife food and cover a short run from rooflines, decks and crawlspaces. Sealing every entry we find, not just the obvious one, is what ends the cycle here.

faqs.q: Do groundhogs do real damage in Glen Burnie?
faqs.a: They do in Anne Arundel County: burrows under decks, sheds and foundation edges undermine slabs and channel water against the house, and garden feeding is heavy from spring through fall. Our crew traps groundhogs at active burrows and backfills and screens the site afterward.

In Odenton's townhome and apartment communities around Piney Orchard and the MARC station, entries are usually building-level problems — a lifted ridge vent or open soffit serves the whole row — so the sealing is typically the owner's responsibility to approve. Removal of the animals already inside comes first so nothing is trapped in the attic, then the report spells out the exclusion work needed to keep the next squirrel or raccoon out.

faqs.q: Are bats common around Piney Orchard and the Odenton lakes?
faqs.a: Yes — the lakes, wetlands, and stream valleys preserved inside Piney Orchard feed clouds of insects at dusk, and big brown and evening bats follow that food into the gable ends and attic peaks of the surrounding subdivisions. Maryland bat work is non-lethal exclusion only, done by an operator whose permit covers bats. We fit one-way exits and seal the remaining gaps, timing larger colonies to the DNR-recommended September 1 to March 1 window when no flightless pups are inside. A single bat loose in a bedroom is handled differently — it is captured and released outside near the home, and we will advise calling the county health department first if anyone may have had contact.

Odenton.wildlife_intro:

Each layer has its own animal. The townhome rows share continuous rooflines, so one squirrel entry at an end unit can mean noise traveling through several attics.

Piney Orchard's lakes and the preserved stream valleys hold raccoons, beaver-influenced wetlands, and heavy bat activity on summer evenings, while the older Odenton core gets skunks under stoops and opossums in crawlspaces. Groundhogs dig along the rail embankments and under the sheds of the larger lots toward Severn and Millersville, and rats appear around the older commercial strips and dumpster areas near the station. Because so many residents rent or live in association-managed communities, Odenton calls often involve a landlord or HOA on the other end of the phone — the inspection report matters as much as the removal, since it documents the entry points and the sealing the building actually needs.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Severna Park porch?

faqs.q: Are bats a problem in Severna Park homes?

faqs.q: Raccoons keep getting on my Pasadena roof from the waterfront side — what is the fix?
faqs.a: On the Magothy and Stoney Creek shorelines, raccoons travel the bulkhead line and climb whatever touches the house: dock posts, leaning trees, and the corners of screened porches. We start by removing the animals using the roof now, then cut back the climb routes we can, cap the chimney, and seal the soffit and roof-junction gaps they were entering through. Securing trash and not leaving pet food or crab scraps on the pier removes the reason they patrol your stretch of shore. Raccoons cannot be relocated in Maryland, so the durable answer is a house they cannot enter and a yard that stops feeding them.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk denning under my Pasadena porch?
faqs.a: Skunks choose the dry, quiet space under porches and slabs in Pasadena's shore communities because the soil is sandy and easy to dig. Keep dogs in after dark and never block the opening while the skunk is still using it — a trapped skunk sprays, and a sealed-in one digs or dies under the house. We confirm the den is active, remove the skunk with covered, low-stress handling, and then trench-screen the porch perimeter so the next skunk cannot dig back in. If young are present in late spring, the plan accounts for them before any screening goes on.

Pasadena.wildlife_intro:
Pasadena occupies the neck of land between the Magothy River and Stoney Creek, and water defines its wildlife work. Waterfront homes in neighborhoods like Green Haven and Sunset Beach sit on low lots with crawlspaces close to the tide line, and raccoons commute along the bulkheads and piers at night, checking boat houses, fish-cleaning stations, and unsecured trash as they go.

Away from the shore, the postwar ranches and cape cods along Mountain Road and Edwin Raynor Boulevard back up to patches of pine and hardwood that hold gray squirrels, and the attic calls follow the acorn crop each fall. Skunks den under the slabs and porches of the older shore communities, groundhogs work the sunny banks along the creeks, and bats roost in the boathouses and older cottages through the summer. Black rat snakes are regulars in Pasadena garages and woodpiles — beneficial, protected, and moved only a short distance when a homeowner insists. The peninsula geography concentrates everything: there is only so much dry ground between the Magothy and Stoney Creek, so homes and habitat are interleaved street by street, and sealing a house here usually means thinking like a raccoon walking the shoreline at low tide.

faqs.q: Moles are ruining my Crofton lawn — what actually works?
faqs.a: Eastern moles tunnel the soft, irrigated soil along Crofton's parkway lawns and golf-course edges hunting earthworms and grubs, and the raised runs appear fastest after rain. Maryland does not require a Wildlife Damage Control Permit for mole work — COMAR exempts mice, moles, rats, and voles — so we will not pretend a license is legally required here. What matters is trapping the active tunnels rather than the old ones, and we show you how we tell them apart by the fresh soil and straight-line runs. Repellents and vibrating stakes rarely hold in this soil; a short, well-placed trapping program on the active runs is what ends the damage.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Crofton?
faqs.a: Crofton pricing hinges on the style of house more than the animal. A townhome with one gable-vent squirrel entry is a compact job; a two-story colonial on a wooded lot with bats in both gable ends, a raccoon chimney, and chewed soffits over the garage is a full roofline project. Chimney caps, vent screening, and any chewed wiring or soiled insulation found in the attic all factor in. We inspect first, show you each entry point and what sealing it involves, and give you the complete figure before any removal begins, so there are no add-ons discovered halfway through.

Crofton.wildlife_intro:
Crofton is a planned community of 1960s and 1970s colonials, ranches, and townhomes wrapped around a parkway and golf course, and its wildlife pattern is pure mature-suburb: the trees planted when the neighborhoods were new are now big enough to bridge onto roofs, and the gray squirrels know every route. Attic calls spike in the older sections each fall as squirrels chew in at soffit returns above the garage additions.

The community's ponds, the Little Patuxent River corridor, and the wooded buffers between sections hold raccoons year-round, and they den in uncapped chimneys and under the low decks that sit close to the ground behind so many Crofton homes. Bats use the gable vents of the two-story colonials in summer, and moles tear up the irrigated lawns along the parkway and around the golf course rough — steady, visible damage that frustrates homeowners even though Maryland treats mole control as permit-exempt work anyone may do. Crofton jobs reward a whole-roofline approach: the same vent style was used across whole streets, so when one gable vent fails, the neighbors' vents are usually the same age and worth a look before the squirrels simply move house.
